title: Kenya Health Ministry launches policy briefs to address pregnancy-related complications
summary: Discussions focused on translating research evidence into practical interventions to improve maternal and newborn survival.
thbAction: Map the news to THB's provider CRM for referral growth, patient lifecycle engagement, and multi-facility relationship management across hospital and provider networks.
contentHtml:
KENYA—The Ministry of Health has launched two policy briefs in Nairobi to address neonatal sepsis and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), conditions that contribute to preventable maternal and newborn deaths in Kenya.

The launch, held under the theme “Know the Causes, Act on Evidence: Ending Preventable Maternal, Newborn, and Child Deaths in Kenya,” brought together government officials, researchers, healthcare partners and media representatives.

Discussions focused on translating research evidence into practical interventions to improve maternal and newborn survival.

Speaking at the event, Director of Family Health Dr Issak Bashir highlighted persistent gaps between existing healthcare policies and their implementation.

He called for greater use of research findings to strengthen clinical practice and improve the delivery of maternal and newborn health services.

The policy briefs were developed by the Ministry’s Division of Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) in partnership with the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Network (CHAMPS).

They provide evidence to guide policy implementation, inform healthcare planning and support coordinated action among government agencies, researchers and development partners.

Focus on newborn care and maternal health

Neonatal sepsis, a serious infection occurring during the first 28 days of life, remains a significant threat to newborn survival.

Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, which include conditions such as pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, also increase the risk of severe complications for mothers and their babies.

Addressing these conditions requires timely diagnosis, appropriate treatment, effective referral systems and access to quality maternal and newborn healthcare.

The policy briefs are intended to support evidence-informed decisions that can strengthen these interventions across Kenya’s health system.

The launch also highlighted the Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere (EWENE) agenda and preparations for World Prematurity Day.

Discussions emphasised the need to improve the quality of care for newborns, identify complications early and provide appropriate follow-up for babies born prematurely.

For healthcare providers and policymakers, the priorities include strengthening newborn care services, improving clinical practices and ensuring continuity of care after discharge.

These interventions also have implications for healthcare resource allocation, workforce capacity and the availability of essential medicines and diagnostic services.

The Ministry’s collaboration with CHAMPS reflects the role of mortality surveillance and research partnerships in identifying gaps in healthcare delivery and informing interventions to reduce preventable deaths.
